new_statements.quote: [p.28] The stress group in Pray may have from one to three syllables, but the majority is monosyllabic. If it has two or more syllables, it has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group. ... [p.91] 4.3.2 Stress. A syllable is said to be stressed if it is more prominent than the surrounding syllables. In Pray, stress is predictable. It is conditioned by the position of the syllable in the stess [sic] group, that is, stress always falls on the last syllable of a stress group.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pray (Prai/T'in) words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (minor presyllable(s) + one major syllable); the stress group (phonological word) of one to three syllables has exactly one stressed syllable, always the final (major) syllable; minor syllables are unstressed with neutral pitch. Stress is predictable, not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None at word level; minor syllables are described as containing no stress (structure 'US'). For Mal, Filbeck 1976 distinguishes three sentence-level stresses with accompanying pitch, not word-level secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only two trisyllabic words found ([si lap'phlap] 'butterfly', [si rak'thak] 'a kind of lizard'), both final-stressed. Pitch is non-phonemic in Pray (phonemic in Mal per Filbeck).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'stress group' (tagmemic hierarchy: intonation group > stress group > syllable > phoneme), effectively the phonological word incl. minor presyllables; described for Pray of Ban Wang Saw, Chon Daen subdistrict, Chiang Klang district, Nan (checked against Ban Nam Lad, Ngob, and Ban Phae Klang, Thung Chang). The same final-major-syllable pattern is stated first-hand for Mal by Filbeck 1976:251 ('all words... are characterised by a single stress' on the major syllable, e.g. [pa'thia?]).
new_statements.identity_note: luaa1235 is a Glottolog BOOKKEEPING languoid: ISO 639-3 [prb] 'Lua'' was retired 2017-01-31 as non-existent (CR 2016-010: "Lua' is a cover term for the Prai and Mal languages"). The archived Ethnologue entry (2016 snapshot, saved) gives alternate names 'East Pua Pray, Pray 2', location Nan province, Bo Kluea district, classification Khmuic > Mal-Phrai; i.e. the referent, insofar as it had one, is a Pray/Prai variety east of Pua = phai1238 (Filbeck 1978:6 notes 'Lua' being adopted as an ethnonym by Pray villages; Jordan-Diller & Diller 2004:20 'They most often refer to their language and their people as Lua'). The quoted statement is Singnoi 1988 on Pray of Ban Wang Saw (Chiang Klang district, checked against Ngob and Thung Chang villages) — Pray generally, not specifically the Bo Kluea villages. CAUTION: the only reference Glottolog attaches to luaa1235 (Charoenma 1980 thesis / 1982 MKS 11 'Wiang Papao Lua') describes a PALAUNGIC language of Ban Pang Chok, Wiang Pa Pao district, Chiang Rai ('Khamet'/Lua, near Lamet, lame1256 area), not the Khmuic T'in 'Lua'' of Nan — a name-based misattachment. Mal (mall1246) and Phai/Pray (phai1238) have their own audit folders; this entry should not be counted as a distinct language (retired code confers no identity).

sources.note: Pray: stress group of 1-3 syllables, nucleus = one stressed syllable, always the LAST syllable (p.28); 'In Pray, stress is predictable... stress always falls on the last syllable of a stress group' (p.91 sec.4.3.2); minor syllables unstressed with neutral pitch; pitch not phonemic in Pray (unlike Mal).

sources.citation: Narumol Charoenma. 1982. The phonologies of a Lampang Lamet and Wiang Papao Lua. Mon-Khmer Studies 11: 35-45.
sources.note: DIFFERENT LANGUAGE (Palaungic 'Lua'/Khamet of Ban Pang Chok, Wiang Pa Pao, Chiang Rai): 'The function and structure of stress groups in Wiang Papao Lua are the same as in Lampang Lamet' (p.41), i.e. 'one strongly stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group' (p.37); two contrastive tones (falling breathy vs normal).

sources.citation: Narumol Charoenma. 1980. The sound systems of Lampang Lamet and Wiang Papao Lua. M.A. thesis, Mahidol University. (the Glottolog-listed reference for luaa1235)
sources.note: Same Palaungic Lua, fuller version: stress group of one or two syllables, nucleus 'one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group' (thesis p.27, Lamet section; Lua section stated to be parallel). Not the Nan T'in 'Lua''.

sources.citation: David Filbeck. 1978. T'in: a historical study. Pacific Linguistics B-49. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-B49.
sources.note: T'in dialects (Mal and Pray) have 'bisyllabic word patterns of minor (stressless) syllable plus major (stressed) syllable' (p.17); vowel length hard to hear outside identical sentence-stress positions (p.~80); pp.5-6 on ethnonyms: Pray also call themselves /lua?/, 'Lua... is being adopted by the Pray in some villages as an ethnonym'.

sources.citation: David Filbeck. 1976. Mal (Thin). In William A. Smalley (ed.), Phonemes and orthography: language planning in ten minority languages of Thailand, 239-257. Pacific Linguistics C-43. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Mal: 'Word structure consists of one major syllable with or without one (or sometimes two) preceding minor syllables. Because words contain only one major syllable, all words, regardless of number of syllables, are characterised by a single stress: /pathia?/ [pa'thia?]' (p.251); minor syllables 'occur only with weak stress'; three sentence stresses with accompanying pitch.
